hints: Picture the carbon skeleton first. Think about what regular shape allows six identical CH groups to be planar with equal angles.
Recall experimental evidence for C-C bond lengths in benzene compared with single and double bonds, and what this tells you about equivalence.
Consider how many regions of electron density each carbon has, and what hybridisation this gives for a trigonal planar carbon.
Think about which orbitals overlap head on to make the framework and which overlap sideways above and below the plane.
walkthrough:
Visualise the planar hexagon**
Imagine six carbons joined in a ring, each with one hydrogen. They all lie flat in the same plane in a perfect regular hexagon. That flat shape lets the p orbitals line up in parallel. Each C-C-C and C-C-H angle is $120^{\circ}$, exactly what you expect for trigonal planar centres.

Make sense of equal bond lengths**
If benzene had alternating single and double bonds, you would see two different lengths. In reality all six C-C bonds are identical, longer than $C=C$ but shorter than $C-C$. That is your clue that the six $\pi$ electrons are delocalised around the whole ring, not fixed in three double bonds.

Assign hybridisation**
Each carbon is bonded to two carbons and one hydrogen, so three $\sigma$ regions. That means promotion and mixing to give three $\text{sp}^2$ hybrid orbitals in the plane, leaving one unhybridised p orbital perpendicular to the plane on each carbon.

Sort out sigma versus pi**
The strong framework is all $\sigma$: $\text{sp}^2$ on carbon overlapping with $\text{sp}^2$ on the next carbon for C-C, and $\text{sp}^2$ on carbon overlapping with s on hydrogen for C-H. Then the six p orbitals overlap sideways, p-p overlap, above and below the ring to give the delocalised $\pi$ system with two $\pi$ electron clouds.

Final answer: Benzene is a planar regular hexagon with all bond angles $120^{\circ}$.
All C-C bonds are the same length, intermediate between single and double.
All carbons are $\text{sp}^2$ hybridised.
$\sigma$ framework: C-C $\text{sp}^2$-$\text{sp}^2$ overlap and C-H $\text{s}$-$\text{sp}^2$ overlap; $\pi$ system: p-p overlap above and below the plane forming a delocalised $\pi$ system.

hints: Remember where the electrons that attack the electrophile come from in benzene, and where a curly arrow for that step must start.
Think about what the ring looks like just after $\text{NO}_2^+$ has joined but before $\text{H}^+$ has left, including charge and which carbon carries two groups.
walkthrough:
Start the first arrow in the pi cloud**
Think of the circle in benzene as your electron source. Draw a curly arrow starting inside the hexagon and pointing to the $\text{N}$ of $^+\text{NO}_2$. That shows a pair of $\pi$ electrons forming the new C-N bond. The ring temporarily loses its aromaticity.

Draw the arenium ion**
You now have a tetrahedral carbon carrying both H and $\text{NO}_2$, and the positive charge spread around the remaining five carbons. Show this as a hexagon with a + charge and with H and $\text{NO}_2$ attached to one carbon. The second stage, which restores aromaticity, is a curly arrow from the C-H bond back into the ring to expel $\text{H}^+$.

Final answer: Curly arrow from $\pi$ system inside hexagon to $\text{NO}_2^+$; curly arrow from C-H bond back into ring to reform $\pi$ system.
Intermediate: cyclohexadienyl cation with $\text{NO}_2$ and H on same carbon, positive charge delocalised in ring.

hints: Focus on the attacking species $\text{NO}_2^+$ and on the fact that the $\text{H}$ it replaces leaves as $\text{H}^+$ with the aromatic ring restored.
walkthrough:
Name by reagent and outcome**
$\text{NO}_2^+$ is electron poor, so it is an electrophile. It substitutes for H on the ring without destroying the benzene $\pi$ system overall. That combination gives electrophilic substitution.
Final answer: Electrophilic substitution

hints: Recall the classic pair of concentrated strong acids used for nitration of benzene.
Think about how $\text{HNO}_3$ acts as a base toward the stronger acid to eventually release $\text{NO}_2^+$ plus water or oxonium species.
walkthrough:
Choose the nitrating mixture**
Nitration needs the powerful electrophile $\text{NO}_2^+$. You generate it in situ from concentrated nitric acid with concentrated sulfuric acid acting as the stronger acid and dehydrating agent.

Write a balanced generation equation**
Sulfuric acid protonates nitric acid, which then loses water: $$\text{HNO}_3 + \text{H}_2\text{SO}_4 \rightarrow \text{NO}_2^+ + \text{H}_2\text{O} + \text{HSO}_4^-$$ Any balanced variant producing $\text{NO}_2^+$ is accepted.

Final answer: Concentrated $\text{HNO}_3$ and concentrated $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$
$\text{HNO}_3 + \text{H}_2\text{SO}_4 \rightarrow \text{NO}_2^+ + \text{H}_2\text{O} + \text{HSO}_4^-$

hints: Think about which metal plus acid combination donates electrons to reduce $\text{-NO}_2$ to $\text{-NH}_2$.
Remember that this reduction needs vigorous heating, so consider the laboratory technique that allows boiling without loss.
walkthrough:
Pick the reducing system**
Changing $\text{-NO}_2$ to $\text{-NH}_2$ is a six electron reduction. Tin in concentrated hydrochloric acid is the standard Paper 4 reagent, supplying electrons with $\text{H}^+$ from the acid.

Add the heating condition**
The mixture needs strong heating to go to completion. Heat, boil or reflux with concentrated acid ensures full reduction to phenylamine.
Final answer: Sn and concentrated $\text{HCl}$, heat under reflux

hints: Remember that the $\text{-NH}_2$ group is strongly activating, so substitution happens three times without a catalyst, and count the $\text{HBr}$ formed.
walkthrough:
Balance the triple substitution**
Phenylamine is so reactive that three $\text{Br}$ atoms replace three ring hydrogens at the 2,4,6 positions. Each substitution consumes one $\text{Br}_2$ and releases one $\text{HBr}$, so: $$\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NH}_2 + 3\text{Br}_2 \rightarrow \text{C}_6\text{H}_2\text{Br}_3\text{NH}_2 + 3\text{HBr}$$

hints: Number the ring with $\text{NH}_2$ as position 1 and locate the three bromines at the two ortho and the para positions.
walkthrough:
Name the trisubstituted product**
With $\text{-NH}_2$ at carbon 1, bromines occupy positions 2, 4 and 6. Combine locants with bromo and the parent phenylamine: 2,4,6-tribromophenylamine.

hints: Think about the colour change of aqueous bromine when it is consumed, plus the physical state of the brominated organic product.
walkthrough:
Link what you see to the chemistry**
Aqueous $\text{Br}_2$ is orange. As it reacts it is used up, so the solution goes colourless. The tribromo product is insoluble in water, so you see a white solid precipitate.
Final answer: Orange bromine water decolourised and white precipitate formed

hints: Start by ordering the three bases from weakest to strongest, thinking about which nitrogen lone pair is least available.
Compare phenylamine with ammonia by asking where the nitrogen lone pair can spread in the aromatic ring.
Compare ethylamine with ammonia by asking how the ethyl group pushes electron density toward nitrogen.
walkthrough:
State the order**
Basicity means readiness to donate a lone pair to $\text{H}^+$. The order is: phenylamine, least basic, then ammonia, then ethylamine, most basic. $$\text{phenylamine} < \text{ammonia} < \text{ethylamine}$$

Explain why phenylamine is weakest**
In phenylamine the nitrogen lone pair overlaps with the ring $\pi$ system and is delocalised into the benzene ring. That pulls electron density away from nitrogen, so the lone pair is much less available to bond to $\text{H}^+$.

Explain why ethylamine is strongest**
In ethylamine the ethyl group is electron donating through the positive inductive effect. It pushes electron density onto nitrogen, making the lone pair more available to accept a proton than the lone pair in ammonia, which has only hydrogens attached.

Final answer: phenylamine < ammonia < ethylamine
Lone pair on N in phenylamine delocalised into benzene ring, less available to accept $\text{H}^+$.
Ethyl group is electron donating by positive inductive effect, lone pair more available to accept $\text{H}^+$ than in ammonia.

hints: Think about what functional group must react with a diamine to make amide links at both ends, so the chain can keep growing.
walkthrough:
Identify the complementary monomer**
A diamine needs a partner with two carboxylic acid type groups to form two amide links. Either a dioic acid or the more reactive dioyl chloride will allow condensation polymerisation.
Final answer: A dioic acid or a dioyl chloride, e.g. hexanedioic acid $\text{HOOC(CH}_2\text{)}_4\text{COOH}$

hints: Sketch alternating diamine and diacid residues joined by $\text{-CO-NH-}$ links, using trailing bonds at the ends to show continuation.
Check that the $\text{C=O}$ of each amide is fully displayed and bracket one complete repeat unit containing one of each residue.
walkthrough:
Build the alternating chain**
Join the diamine $\text{H}_2\text{NCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{NH}_2$ to the dioic acid with loss of water at each end. Alternate them: acid, amine, acid, amine. Show four residues in total, two of each, with trailing bonds at both ends to indicate the polymer continues.

Display the amide and mark the repeat**
Draw each link as $\text{-C(=O)-NH-}$ with the $\text{C=O}$ fully shown. Then bracket or label one repeat unit, for example $$\text{-CO-(CH}_2\text{)}_4\text{-CO-NH-(CH}_2\text{)}_3\text{-NH-}$$ which contains one diacid residue plus one diamine residue linked by amides.

Final answer: Section with two diamine residues and two diacid residues alternating, e.g. $\text{-CO-(CH}_2\text{)}_4\text{-CO-NH-(CH}_2\text{)}_3\text{-NH-CO-(CH}_2\text{)}_4\text{-CO-NH-(CH}_2\text{)}_3\text{-NH-}$ with trailing bonds; amide $\text{C=O}$ fully displayed; one repeat unit $\text{-CO-(CH}_2\text{)}_4\text{-CO-NH-(CH}_2\text{)}_3\text{-NH-}$ identified.
